messages.subject: DIF directionality
messages.body_plain:
Hello Phil,

Quick question about direction of bias using DIF().  Using this code:

model_anchor <- multipleGroup(items_firstlang, model = Q1, group = firstlang,
                              invariance = c(itemnames[c(9,11,14,15,25,28,30,36)], 'free_means', 'free_var'))

anchor <- DIF(model_anchor, c('a1', 'd'),
              items2test = c(1:8,10,12:13,16:24,26,27,29,31:35,37:51), plotdif = TRUE)
anchor

Several items showed DIF (please see attached plots).  Looking at plots of rmc12 and rmc24, the bias is in favor of different groups (for rmc12, the favor is Yes and for rmc24 it's No).

Here is output for those two items:

$rmc12
       AIC     AICc    SABIC       HQ      BIC    logLik     X2  df   p
1 629807.6 629823.8 630936.7 630491.0 631826.5 -314623.8    NaN NaN NaN
2 629786.2 629802.6 630923.4 630474.5 631819.5 -314611.1 25.428   2   0

$rmc24
       AIC     AICc    SABIC       HQ      BIC    logLik     X2  df   p
1 629816.0 629832.2 630945.1 630499.4 631834.9 -314628.0    NaN NaN NaN
2 629786.2 629802.6 630923.4 630474.5 631819.5 -314611.1 33.827   2   0

Is there any way to interpret the output for direction of bias? I realize DRF() does this with signed/unsigned but I was wondering if DIF() does as well.

Also, on a related note, the attached plots seem to show only a portion of the DIF-evident items. There are items with p<.05 in the output that didn't show up in the plots. I am wondering if I am missing something about which items are plotted with plotdif=TRUE.

Thank you as always!
Jeanne

> 1 629807.6 629823.8 630936.7 630491.0 631826.5 -314623.8    NaN NaN NaN
> 2 629786.2 629802.6 630923.4 630474.5 631819.5 -314611.1 25.428   2   0
>

>        AIC     AICc    SABIC       HQ      BIC    logLik     X2  df   p
> 1 629816.0 629832.2 630945.1 630499.4 631834.9 -314628.0    NaN NaN NaN
> 2 629786.2 629802.6 630923.4 630474.5 631819.5 -314611.1 33.827   2   0
>
>
> Is there any way to interpret the output for direction of bias? I realize DRF() does this with signed/unsigned but I was wondering if DIF() does as well.

Not particularly no, these are just reports from the anova() function comparing nested parameter differences. While I like the idea of printing the parameter sets to actually visualize and inspect these properties first-hand, it may be better just to use the "return_models" logical flag and sift through the item objects where DIF was detected. In that way, you could still use things like the DRF function, create plots, print the comparable coefficients, and so on.

>
> Also, on a related note, the attached plots seem to show only a portion of the DIF-evident items. There are items with p<.05 in the output that didn't show up in the plots. I am wondering if I am missing something about which items are plotted with plotdif=TRUE.

I don't see a plot here, sorry. But according to the documentation:

plotdif --- logical; create item plots for items that are displaying DIF according to the seq_stat criteria? Only available for 'add' type schemes

The seq_stat criteria here is 'SABIC', so only those items are plotted. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Correlated errors
messages.body_plain:
With categorical models there's no residual variance terms present, so residual covariation doesn't make sense either. You can accomplish the same effect though by including a new factor that loads on the two items with residual variance, and constrain the slope parameters to be equal for this new factor, like so:

model <- "
G = 1-30   # 30 item test
resid = 1,2    # residual covariation between items 1 and 2
CONSTRAIN = (1, 2, a2)" ## constrain the a2 slopes to be equal

Phil

I'm using DRF to analyze a literacy exam, and I have what sort of looks like an odd plot (please see attached). The error area and the estimated DRF line do not overlap in a section. Note: I was using mirtCluster if that makes a difference.  I would greatly appreciate any advice!

messages.subject: comparing instrument reliability of an adaptive test for different groups
messages.subject_clean: comparing instrument reliability of an adaptive test for different groups
messages.body_plain:
More than 10k people filled out an online adaptive ability test.
The test results are scored with mirt.
I would like to see if the reliability of the instrument was the same for a small subgroup than for others with similar ability level.
The average ability of this group is much higher than for the rest of my test-takers.
Could you recommend a test for this?

messages.subject: Re: upper and lower bound of the scale scores (different values)
messages.subject_clean: upper and lower bound of the scale scores (different values)
messages.body_plain:
You can't, at least not the way that max_theta has been organized internally. Why not just manually truncate these values after estimation anyway?

fs <- fscores(mod)
fs <- ifelse(fs < -2.5, -2.5, fs)
fs <- ifelse(fs > 4.5, 4.5, fs)
head(fs)

If all you need these for is some type of truncation then these can be applied post-hoc.

Phil

messages.subject: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
messages.subject_clean: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

I am working with some questionnaires from several datasets that contain data collected for a long timespan (10 to 40 years). In some datasets, the responses were collected in a longitudinal manner and in some in a cross-sectional manner.

I have analyzed the data using both confirmatory factor analysis and item response theory. These analyses tell me that there is no measurement invariance. In other words, CFA tells me that the factor loadings change over the years of questionnaire administartion (they tend to increase), while IRT tells me that the item parameters also change over the years.

The papers that I have read tell me that it's not really justifiable to look at how the scores change over the years if there is no measurement invariance over time. However, I was wondering if it may somehow still be possible to do this. One thing that comes to my mind is scaling using IRT, which I know that I can do using your mirt package using the multipleGroup function in which I would specify the names of anchor items. However, the issue that I have is that there are no anchor items, or to put it more straightforward, all items are anchor items - the questionnaire did not change over the years. Therefore I was wondering if it would make sense to use the multipleGroup function (with the year as a group) and to specify all items as anchor items in order to see how the measured construct changes over the years. I would also free the latent means using mirt.model and then plot the latent means over years.

If this is not the right approach, is there anything you would recommend?

messages.subject: Re: a few questions around DRF
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeanne,

If there is crossing at the 0 y-axis location then there is always a possibility that sDRF could be n.s., depending on the (joint) density shape of the underlying theta distribution. You have to interpret this measure as the product between the response difference between the groups (as this plot shows at each theta), allowing for cancellation affects for sDRF, while also weighting by the proportion of individuals at these locations. Hence, if very few individual propagate at theta = -4, then this large difference may matter very little to the majority of the individuals. So in actuality, locations closer to the theta = 0 location often matter more than the differences in the tail of these plots (not to say that there isn't differences in these locations, as these plots show, just that the proportion of individuals who would witness this type of bias is rather negligible). sDRF, along with statistics such as SIBTEST and the Mantel-Hazel statistics suffer from this general cancellation problem, so unless you are studying Rasch-type models their usefulness becomes less clear. HTH.

Phil

> On Aug 19, 2018, at 1:46 AM, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Jeanne,
>
> If there is crossing at the 0 y-axis location then there is always a possibility that sDRF could be n.s., depending on the (joint) density shape of the underlying theta distribution. You have to interpret this measure as the product between the response difference between the groups (as this plot shows at each theta), allowing for cancellation affects for sDRF, while also weighting by the proportion of individuals at these locations. Hence, if very few individual propagate at theta = -4, then this large difference may matter very little to the majority of the individuals. So in actuality, locations closer to the theta = 0 location often matter more than the differences in the tail of these plots (not to say that there isn't differences in these locations, as these plots show, just that the proportion of individuals who would witness this type of bias is rather negligible). sDRF, along with statistics such as SIBTEST and the Mantel-Hazel statistics suffer from this general cancellation problem, so unless you are studying Rasch-type models their usefulness becomes less clear. HTH.

> > > > > > > > > > Does this interpretation hold for polytomous items? I noticed the MG output indicates that "Item re-scored so that all values are within a distance of 1” — does this take care of the interpretation of the effect size for polytomous items?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Sure does. For polytomous items these are with respect to the item scoring function, which is the generalisation of the probability interpretation for dichotomous items (the scoring and probability functions for dichotomous items are identical).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Thank you!
> > > > > > > > > > Jeanne
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > On Jul 1, 2018, at 11:35 PM, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >

> > > > > > > > > > > On Sun, Jul 1, 2018 at 3:34 PM Jeanne Sinclair <jeanneh...@gmail.com <http://gmail.com/>> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > > > Hi Phil,
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Thank you once again for the great feedback and support on the mirt package! I am working on analysing literacy achievement data using the DRF statistics and have a few questions I'd very much appreciate your help with. Apologies for any questions that are naive.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Here's a sample of the syntax or reference:
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > model_anchorpoetrysocialmediasongs<- multipleGroup(DIF1and6items, model = Q1, group = grouppoetrysocialmediasongs,
> > > > > > > > > > > >                                                    invariance = c(itemnames[c(6:11,41)],
> > > > > > > > > > > >                                                                   'free_means', 'free_var'), SE=T)
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > dialogDRF2poetrysocialmediasongs= DRF(model_anchorpoetrysocialmediasongs, focal_items = c(21:25,42,43), plot = F,draws=500)
> > > > > > > > > > > > dialogDRF2poetrysocialmediasongs
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Output:
> > > > > > > > > > > >      n_focal_items        stat      CI_2.5     CI_97.5        X2 df           p
> > > > > > > > > > > > sDRF             7 -0.07664762 -0.15114407 0.004747429  3.900895  1 0.048260391
> > > > > > > > > > > > uDRF             7  0.13499792  0.06517565 0.213141560 12.366079  2 0.002064145
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > (Please also see attached plot of this output).
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 1. If I understand correctly, the 2018 Psychometrika article ("Model-based"...) suggests that non-studied items are included in the DRF analyses. Can you please explain a bit further how non-studied items are included? In the provided syntax I understand they are used for modeling the configural MG model as separate groups but I am not sure how they are included in the DRF analysis.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Non-studied items are really just auxiliary information and don't play a part in the model other than improving statistical power and introducing bias/less efficiency in the estimates. These have been present in many other analysis as well (like those in the DIF() function), in that they represent all the items in a fitted IRT model that were not in the focal set (the item to test for DIF) and anchor set (the items explicitly declared as anchors in the fitted model). I wouldn't worry much about this one, I just needed to give them a name to contrast these with the SIBTEST approach.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 2. Can inferences about both difficulty and discrimination be generated based on these sDRF and uDRF statistics / attached plot? Or just difficulty?
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Neither. These are about the *model-implied bias*, and are detached from any parameter interpretation. That's what makes them so nice for effect size interpretation, because sDRF always represents the average scoring between groups for a given (set) of items, while uDRF is the average deviation bias between the given (set) of items.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Are sDRF and uDRF statistics calculated as the average across entire theta? (I read that a subset of theta can be calculated instead but I wanted to be sure.) And, are the uDRF and sDRF stats printed above effect sizes that can be interpreted similarly to Cohen's d?
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Effectively, you can interpreted them as such. For example, a uDRF = 0.1 with only one focal item (i.e., DIF) says that the item response functions will differ on average by about .1 points. So at any given location across the range of theta, we would expect the two groups to show a scoring different of 0.1. The same interpretation exists for sDRF, but with respect to the balance of scoring form.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 4. If the focal group selection is arbitrary, do I assume a negatively signed value of sDRF as above refers to invariance in favor of group 1 (the reference group)?
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Correct.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 5. In the attached plot, which is related to the above output, the values on higher levels of theta appear to be more reliable. These are biased in favor of group 1 (the reference group), correct? As the area under the curve is greater on the lower end of theta (in favor of focal group), is it the lack of accuracy in the lower region of theta that makes the overall sDRF in favor of the reference group? Is this what is meant by marginal density of the latent trait distribution (here, that there are few cases with very low theta values)?
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > This plot is really the conditional bias effect of of bias across theta, whereas the DRF statistics try to marginalize this entire response function into single statistics (and may do so poorly). Hence, uDRF is telling you the average difference between these functions, while sDRF is telling you the average while allowing for cancellation effects (hence, the global scoring bias observed....which could potentially cancel out as nearly happens in this plot, and is why sDRF was so close to 0 in your output).
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > 6. Lastly, I have five groups, one of which is reference. I have run independent IRT models like the one above for each group and then subsequent DRF for each bundle for each 2-group IRT model. Is that the correct procedure for multiple groups?
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > For now, yes. I'm working on many extensions to this work, one of which is incorporating more than two groups at once. But for now, there's nothing really wrong with your approach, and in many ways is quite favorable. HTH.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Thank you!

messages.subject: Re: doubts about fscores

Exploratory models are only unique up to a linear rotation. So the total scores may not correlate with the factor scores unless suitable transformations are applied, and possibly multiplied by -1 to flip the signs. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
messages.subject_clean: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Aug 18, 2018 at 11:02 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear Phil,
>
> I am working with some questionnaires from several datasets that contain data collected for a long timespan (10 to 40 years). In some datasets, the responses were collected in a longitudinal manner and in some in a cross-sectional manner.
>
> I have analyzed the data using both confirmatory factor analysis and item response theory. These analyses tell me that there is no measurement invariance. In other words, CFA tells me that the factor loadings change over the years of questionnaire administartion (they tend to increase), while IRT tells me that the item parameters also change over the years.

How does this tell you there is no measurement invariance? If the properties of the population change, such as there is more variability in the latent trait distribution/mean-score increases, then changes in the observed item parameters would be expected. It's only possible to make this type of conclusion if you are certain the population latent trait values themselves should theoretically remain constant over time; otherwise, you'd have to do some item parameter equating.

>
> The papers that I have read tell me that it's not really justifiable to look at how the scores change over the years if there is no measurement invariance over time. However, I was wondering if it may somehow still be possible to do this. One thing that comes to my mind is scaling using IRT, which I know that I can do using your mirt package using the multipleGroup function in which I would specify the names of anchor items. However, the issue that I have is that there are no anchor items, or to put it more straightforward, all items are anchor items - the questionnaire did not change over the years. Therefore I was wondering if it would make sense to use the multipleGroup function (with the year as a group) and to specify all items as anchor items in order to see how the measured construct changes over the years. I would also free the latent means using mirt.model and then plot the latent means over years.
>
> If this is not the right approach, is there anything you would recommend?

Unfortunately, I don't think I'd recommend this 100%, unless under special conditions. The longitudinal aspect of the model suggests that individuals appeared in more than one time point, while in multipleGroup() the individuals are assumed to be independent. More than likely you'd have to setup some type of longitudinal model, like so: https://philchalmers.github.io/mirt/html/Longitudinal-IRT.html. This example isn't the best in that the constraints use an older format (I should replace it with the current syntax mode....but haven't found the time yet), so you'll have to try to determine what's going on from the output coefficients. Similar analyses are also possible with SEM, and if you can make the assumption that the items types are strictly ordinal (so that the graded response model is reasonable) then it may be best to start with that method before moving to IRT, primarily for estimation-based reasons. HTH.

Phil

Hi Phil,

Thank you for the answer to my last question - I found the two-tier bifactor model as a good compromise. Now, I am trying to assess how well a unidimensional model fits the data by comparing observed and expected marginal category response rates and found something peculiar when I compared the test scores that I don't understand: when I generate the expected scores using the EAP algorithm it overpredicts below the midpoint and underpredicts over the midpoint. Meanwhile, expected scores seem to be predicted fairly well with the ML algorithm. Why is this?

Theta <- fscores(fit, method="EAP", full.scores = T)
obs <- rowSums(data)
exp <- expected.test(fit,Theta)

Theta <- fscores(fit, method="ML", full.scores = T)
obs <- rowSums(data)
exp <- expected.test(fit,Theta)

Also,how would you recommend to compute the marginal category response probabilities? I have tried the method below, but it is too accurate to be reasonable (high accuracy even for poor models).

library(mirtCAT)
Theta <- fscores(fit,method="EAP")
obsPattern <- data
expPattern <- data.frame( generate_pattern(fit,Theta) )
prop.table(table(obsPattern[,1])) #1 is item 1
prop.table(table(expPattern[,1]))

Best,
Rico

messages.subject: items of type "none"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I'm trying to create a multi-dim CAT and most things work like a charm, but I have a question regarding the inclusion of type "none" questions.
Following Scenario:
I want to create a CAT with two blocks with 50 questions each and an "instructions"-Page between block1 and block2. To include the instructions page, I created a type "none" question with an item stem that consists of the instructions for block2. Thus, I created an according data.frame for the questions with 101 rows, rows 1:50 belonging to the questions of block 1, row 51 being the type none instruction page, and rows 52:101 belonging to the questions of block 2. This works like a charm for a non-adaptive,sequential test.
However, if I want to create an adaptive test with an underlying model (based on prior responses to the 100 items), I have to define an underlying model that should look mostly like this:

"F1 = 1-50
 F2 = 52-101"

However, if I use this model, I have to provide a dataset with answers for 101 questions and using an "NA"-Column for the type none question 51 does not work, giving me an error message (see example code). Still, leaving the type none item out while creating the model also does not make sense.

So how to proceed with type none-questions when creating a mirt-model?

Thanks in advance,

Daniel

Example Code (generating random responses for questions 1:50 and 52:101) and trying to create the mirt-model afterwards

x<-c(rep(1,100),rep(0,100))
V1<-sample(x,100)
for (i in 1:100){
  V1<-cbind(V1,sample(x,100))
}
data<-V1
data<-cbind(data[,1:50],NA,data[,51:100])
colnames(data)<-1:101

model <- mirt.model("F1 = 1-50
                     F2 = 52-101")
mirt(data,model,guess=0.25, method="EM",technical=list(NCYCLES=15))->mirt_model

messages.subject: Re: items of type "none"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

I understand what you are asking, and can certainly offer some advice here, but want to make sure I get the intention right first. To start, do you have real data that corresponds the CAT items you are trying to make? In other words, do you already have access to a dataset that has 100 items (whereas your CAT requires 101 item structures, as you are aware of)?

If so, then fit the data normally using the mirt() function, and translate these parameters into the structure you need via the generate.mirt_object() function. That way, you know that these "ghosted" items are not included in the fitted model, and so that you have complete control over where these 'none' types go during the new model translation definition. Admittedly, this is a bit awkward, and I'm open to suggestions on how to improve this format. HTH.

Phil

On Wed, Aug 22, 2018 at 9:15 AM <rico...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thank you for the quick reply. I was looking into these statistics and the reason I wanted to take it further was because the results of the S_X2 statistics was a bit surprising. Looking at the S_X2 tables I find that the observed and expected frequencies are matching well (table in attached picture), but the S_X2-test is still highly significant (I have a sample size around 30000, but even with a random subsamples of 1000, all items start to misfit very much). The M2 indices show good fit, and individual item residuals are all around 0.05 (both for M2 and LD). Am missing something?
>
> itemfit(fit,S_X2.tables=T)[[1]] #O.org
> itemfit(fit,S_X2.tables=T)[[2]] #E.org

This sounds reasonable to me. M2 and other linear-dependence statistics are very underpowered at detecting misfitting items, particularly because their purpose is in studying the expected behaviour of uni+bivariate covariance components. The itemfit statistics are more isolated and better at detecting isolated misfitting items, so what you are seeing here is reasonable. So, what you are seeing here is, unsurprisingly, that the IRT functional forms do not fit *exactly* to the empirical data, though your tables do indicate that the functions may be reasonably close. I've found inspecting the two-step itemfit plots (via the empirical.plot input) useful for gauging the severity of misfit, but only if the test length is reasonably long. The S-X2 tables are slightly harder to visualize, mainly because there's only a finite number of empirical bins that can be constructed, but effectively give similar information when plotted. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Examinees total size in equating different examns
messages.subject_clean: Examinees total size in equating different examns
messages.body_plain:
Hello Phill, It`s me again!

I have a doubt about the equating proccess of MIRT.

Suppose I have three examns, applied in three consecutive years, for three different student pools. These 3 examns have some common itens, and the parameters are fixed step by step, from year 1 to two 3.

For the first year I have 100,000 examinees.
For the second year I have 500 examinees.
For the third year I have 1200 examinees.

Now suppose I have made my first equating procces, linking year 1 and year 2 examns.
Do I need to expand (or change, in some way) the size of examinees for year 2 in order to guarantee the correct parameters estimation and fixing?

In BILOG-MG, It was necessary to expand the number of examinees of the second examn (in order to make the number of examinees in examn 2 equal to the number of examinees in examn 1) to make sure the fixed parameters of the second examn were truly fixed.

The scenario, then, would be:
1st year: 100,000 examinees
2nd year: 100,00 examinees (500 real examinees * 20)
3rd year: 1,200 examinees

I've faced this problem because the fixed parameters outputed by bilog changed slightly, and this change increased at each step of the equating procces.

In MIRT, the outputed fixed parameters don`t change at all from the numbers that I inputed.

If my input was a1(1.2) - d (2.3) - g(0.2), for a single fixed item, then the output is a1(1.2) - d (2.3) - g(0.2) - exactly the same. Does this occur because the MIRT doesn`t allow MIRT to change the fixed parameters during the equating procces (even slightly) or does this happen because MIRT allows parameters to change slightly (just like BILOG-MG) but then the MIRT prints the original inputed fixed parameters?

Thanks in Advance for your help!

Best regards,

Flavio

messages.subject: Re: Scoring of multiple answer items
messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

just as a short addendum to your answer to my initial question:

AnswerFuns #1

function(text) all(text %in% c("Strongly Disagree", "Disagree"))

This function checks if the answers provided by the participants are elements of "Strongly Disagree", "Disagree". It will thus return TRUE as long as participants only check correct answers. Yet, it will also return TRUE is participants don't check all correct answers.

AnswerFuns #2
function(text) setequal(text,c("Strongly Disagree", "Disagree"))
This function checks if the answers provided by the participants equal the correct answers "Strongly Disagree", "Disagree". It will thus return TRUE only if the participants check all correct answers.

AnswerFuns #1 thus does not fully fulfill the intended scoring asked for in my initial post ( "Score an item with 1 point if and only if all correct answers are checked.") and I wanted to clarify this so that future readers don't make a mistake here.

Thanks again @Phil.

Daniel

Hi Phil,

yes, you understood everything perfectly well and using generate.mirt_object() worked perfectly.

For future users:
This is what the new code would look like (minimal working example):

require('mirtCAT')

#generate some random answers
x<-c(rep(1,100),rep(0,100))
V1<-sample(x,100)
for (i in 1:99){
  V1<-cbind(V1,sample(x,100))
}

#define df as dataset containing 100 answers (rows) for 100 items (columns)
df<-V1
colnames(df)<-1:100

#define mirt.model for the 100 items
model <- mirt.model("F1 = 1-50
                    F2 = 51-100")

#calculate model for 100 items
full_model<-mirt(df,model,guess=0.25, method="EM",technical=list(NCYCLES=15))

##Now lets insert the type-none-item

#get coefficients for the 100 items
mod_1<-coef(full_model, simplify=TRUE)$items

#create a coefficients row for the type-none-item
mod_none_questions<-matrix(NA,ncol=ncol(mod_1),nrow=1)

#bind everything together in the appropriate order
mod_ges<- rbind(mod_1[1:50,],mod_none_questions,mod_1[51:100,])

#create final model for mirtCAT
mod_final <- generate.mirt_object(mod_ges, itemtype = c(rep('2PL', nrow(mod_ges))))

#check results
coef(mod_final,simplify=T)

Additionally I created a custom NextItemFunction to make sure the CAT will first choose from items 1:50, then administer the type-none-question and the choose from items 52:101.

Best, Daniel

Great, thank you for a really clear answer. Forgive me if this sounds a bit crude, but if S_X2 indicates complete item misfit when observed and expected frequencies are this similar, what information does it really provide when analyzing empirical data? I mean with larger sample sizes could one ever expect the model to exactly fit the data, and wouldn't an effect size measure be more informative? I find the plots are really good (your package is awesome), but the problem is that I mainly work with multidimensional models for which there are no obs/exp itemplots.

Last question: Would marginal category probabilities computed from the S-X2 tables be a fair measure of model fit? Or even, would RMSE of probabilities computed per category add something?

Best,
Rico

The M2 indices show good fit, and individual item residuals are all around 0.05 (both for M2 and LD). Am missing something?

So, what you are seeing here is, unsurprisingly, that the IRT functional forms do not fit *exactly* to the empirical data, though your tables do indicate that the functions may be reasonably close. all(c("Strongly Disagree", "Disagree") %in% text)

messages.subject_clean: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

Thank you for the examples. I will do my best to produce such models and apply them to my data. However, I am a bit confused about the answer and I was trying to wrap my head around it. If the population-mean score of the latent trait is increasing, shouldn't that only impact the person parameter (Theta) and not the item parameters? Isn't one of the advantages of IRT over CTT that the person parameters and item parameters are independent? In other words, if the item parameters change over the years, doesn't that tell us that the very way in which people respond to items has changed (and not necessarily the person parameters/population means)?

On Tuesday, August 21, 2018 at 4:15:53 AM UTC+1, Phil Chalmers wrote:
>
> On Sat, Aug 18, 2018 at 11:02 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear Phil,
> >
> > I am working with some questionnaires from several datasets that contain data collected for a long timespan (10 to 40 years). In some datasets, the responses were collected in a longitudinal manner and in some in a cross-sectional manner.
> >
> > I have analyzed the data using both confirmatory factor analysis and item response theory. These analyses tell me that there is no measurement invariance. In other words, CFA tells me that the factor loadings change over the years of questionnaire administartion (they tend to increase), while IRT tells me that the item parameters also change over the years.
>
> How does this tell you there is no measurement invariance? If the properties of the population change, such as there is more variability in the latent trait distribution/mean-score increases, then changes in the observed item parameters would be expected. It's only possible to make this type of conclusion if you are certain the population latent trait values themselves should theoretically remain constant over time; otherwise, you'd have to do some item parameter equating.
>
> >

messages.subject_clean: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
messages.body_plain:
Just because the item parameters and latent trait values are independent does not mean that their scale is constant. This is why IRT models often set the latent trait identification to have a mean of 0, variance of 1 (same problem occurs in SEM). If some other values were chosen then these would in fact affect the item parameters. This is actually the reason why *linking* parameter sets across multiple groups is required, because any mean/variance differences will make the parameters non-equivalent.

If you are still having trouble with this idea, consider playing around with the example code in the multipleGroup() function, generating data with different latent trait distributions, and see how the single group item parameters can change. Also, topics on DIF will illuminating as well. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Yes, but I believe the fscores() function does not support multiple-group models given the response.pattern input.
You may have to use the extract.group() function to create a single-model extraction, and then use this in conjunction with fscores() and the response patterns you want scored. E.g.,

#########################
set.seed(12345)
a <- matrix(abs(rnorm(15,1,.3)), ncol=1)
d <- matrix(rnorm(15,0,.7),ncol=1)
itemtype <- rep('2PL', nrow(a))
N <- 1000
dataset1 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype)
dataset2 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype, mu = .1, sigma = matrix(1.5))
dat <- rbind(dataset1, dataset2)
group <- c(rep('D1', N), rep('D2', N))
models <- 'F1 = 1-15'

mod_configural <- multipleGroup(dat, models, group = group)
group.1 <- extract.group(mod_configural, 1) #extract first group
coef(group.1, simplify=TRUE)

pat <- sample(0:1, 15, TRUE)
fscores(group.1, response.pattern = pat)

#####################

HTH.

Phil

You have to interpret this measure as the product between the response difference between the groups (as this plot shows at each theta), allowing for cancellation affects for sDRF, while also weighting by the proportion of individuals at these locations. Hence, if very few individual propagate at theta = -4, then this large difference may matter very little to the majority of the individuals. So in actuality, locations closer to the theta = 0 location often matter more than the differences in the tail of these plots (not to say that there isn't differences in these locations, as these plots show, just that the proportion of individuals who would witness this type of bias is rather negligible). sDRF, along with statistics such as SIBTEST and the Mantel-Hazel statistics suffer from this general cancellation problem, so unless you are studying Rasch-type models their usefulness becomes less clear. > > > > > > > > > > > > Neither. These are about the *model-implied bias*, and are detached from any parameter interpretation. That's what makes them so nice for effect size interpretation, because sDRF always represents the average scoring between groups for a given (set) of items, while uDRF is the average deviation bias between the given (set) of items.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > 3. Are sDRF and uDRF statistics calculated as the average across entire theta? (I read that a subset of theta can be calculated instead but I wanted to be sure.) And, are the uDRF and sDRF stats printed above effect sizes that can be interpreted similarly to Cohen's d?
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Effectively, you can interpreted them as such. For example, a uDRF = 0.1 with only one focal item (i.e., DIF) says that the item response functions will differ on average by about .1 points. So at any given location across the range of theta, we would expect the two groups to show a scoring different of 0.1. The same interpretation exists for sDRF, but with respect to the balance of scoring form.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > 4. If the focal group selection is arbitrary, do I assume a negatively signed value of sDRF as above refers to invariance in favor of group 1 (the reference group)?
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Correct.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > 5. In the attached plot, which is related to the above output, the values on higher levels of theta appear to be more reliable. These are biased in favor of group 1 (the reference group), correct? As the area under the curve is greater on the lower end of theta (in favor of focal group), is it the lack of accuracy in the lower region of theta that makes the overall sDRF in favor of the reference group? Is this what is meant by marginal density of the latent trait distribution (here, that there are few cases with very low theta values)?
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > This plot is really the conditional bias effect of of bias across theta, whereas the DRF statistics try to marginalize this entire response function into single statistics (and may do so poorly). Hence, uDRF is telling you the average difference between these functions, while sDRF is telling you the average while allowing for cancellation effects (hence, the global scoring bias observed....which could potentially cancel out as nearly happens in this plot, and is why sDRF was so close to 0 in your output).
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > 6. Lastly, I have five groups, one of which is reference. I have run independent IRT models like the one above for each group and then subsequent DRF for each bundle for each 2-group IRT model. Is that the correct procedure for multiple groups?
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > For now, yes. I'm working on many extensions to this work, one of which is incorporating more than two groups at once. But for now, there's nothing really wrong with your approach, and in many ways is quite favorable. HTH.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Phil
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Thank you!
> > > > > > > > > > > > > Jeanne

messages.subject: Re: a few questions around DRF
messages.body_plain:
The 'group' input gets translated into a factor, so if the input is a character then the reference group is the first level of the following

group <- factor(group)

You can make this explicit by passing a factor with the levels you want. See below:

set.seed(12345)
a <- matrix(abs(rnorm(15,1,.3)), ncol=1)
d <- matrix(rnorm(15,0,.7),ncol=1)
itemtype <- rep('2PL', nrow(a))
N <- 1000
dataset1 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype)
dataset2 <- simdata(a, d, N, itemtype, mu = .1, sigma = matrix(1.5))
dat <- rbind(dataset1, dataset2)
group <- factor(c(rep('D1', N), rep('D2', N)))
models <- 'F1 = 1-15'
group2 <- factor(group, levels = c('D2', 'D1'))

table(group)
table(group2)

mod_configural <- multipleGroup(dat, models, group = group)
mod_configural2 <- multipleGroup(dat, models, group = group2)
coef(mod_configural, simplify=TRUE)
coef(mod_configural2, simplify=TRUE)

Phil

Great, thank you. I believe they do add useful information, but agree that it is hard to set the threshold for acceptable fit. I did some testing on a 14-item scale modeled as unidimensional, 2 correlated latent traits and bifactor with 2 specific factors. I have attached the results which show model loadings, M2* overall fit, Item fit (including RMSEA), average M2* residual per item and average LDG2 residual per item, obs vs expected S_X2 proportion per category for two items, and finally, the absolute difference between the observed and expected proportions for both items. Quite interesting to see how small the S_x2-based differences were between models compared to for example the LDG2 residuals. Like you mentioned earlier, i think these plots can be rather helpful since they allow visualizing obs/exp for multidimensional models.

Best,
Rico

messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

I think I understood why the change in the parameters doesn't necessarily tell us that there is measurement invariance. However, I am still a bit confused about the longitudinal models in your example and I would like to ask for your help again. Specifically, I have these questions:

1.) In your examples, you've set constraints on item parameters. Does this allow us to make inferences on the trajectory of the latent construct over time (i.e., is this equivalent to equating)?
2.) Is it justifiable to set the constraints on parameters? I imagine that you would have to compute a constrained model and a non-constrained model and compare them. In that case, how would we proceed if the models differ significantly?

On Saturday, August 25, 2018 at 10:40:44 PM UTC+1, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> Just because the item parameters and latent trait values are independent does not mean that their scale is constant. This is why IRT models often set the latent trait identification to have a mean of 0, variance of 1 (same problem occurs in SEM). If some other values were chosen then these would in fact affect the item parameters. This is actually the reason why *linking* parameter sets across multiple groups is required, because any mean/variance differences will make the parameters non-equivalent.
>
> If you are still having trouble with this idea, consider playing around with the example code in the multipleGroup() function, generating data with different latent trait distributions, and see how the single group item parameters can change. Also, topics on DIF will illuminating as well. HTH.
>
> Phil
>
>
> On Sat, Aug 25, 2018 at 4:22 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear Phil,
> >
> > Thank you for the examples. I will do my best to produce such models and apply them to my data. However, I am a bit confused about the answer and I was trying to wrap my head around it. If the population-mean score of the latent trait is increasing, shouldn't that only impact the person parameter (Theta) and not the item parameters? Isn't one of the advantages of IRT over CTT that the person parameters and item parameters are independent? In other words, if the item parameters change over the years, doesn't that tell us that the very way in which people respond to items has changed (and not necessarily the person parameters/population means)?
> >
> > On Tuesday, August 21, 2018 at 4:15:53 AM UTC+1, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> > >
> > > On Sat, Aug 18, 2018 at 11:02 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Dear Phil,
> > > >
> > > > I am working with some questionnaires from several datasets that contain data collected for a long timespan (10 to 40 years). In some datasets, the responses were collected in a longitudinal manner and in some in a cross-sectional manner.
> > > >
> > > > I have analyzed the data using both confirmatory factor analysis and item response theory. These analyses tell me that there is no measurement invariance. In other words, CFA tells me that the factor loadings change over the years of questionnaire administartion (they tend to increase), while IRT tells me that the item parameters also change over the years.
> > >
> > > How does this tell you there is no measurement invariance? messages.subject: Sum score reliability
messages.body_plain:
Hello. I used mirt to investigate factor validity, however the test will be used in practice under CTT framework and sum scores will be used for decisions (shame on it, but there are some practical reasons which I cannot influence). So I would like to provide reliability estimate of sum score based on the mirt result.

Under factor analysis, I would use omega coefficient based on ordinal CFA (which works with loadings and residual variances) and I would take thresholds in the account, which leads to the reliability of sum score estimated using ordinal model.

Under IRT, reliability estimates are usually reliabilities of the factor scores estimates, not of the sum score. Am I right that if I use e.g. fscores(fitted_model, method="EAPsum", returnER = T) , I get reliability of factor scores estimated using the total sum score only? And am I right that this reliability estimate is exactly the same as the reliability of sum score itself?

Best, Hynek

Thanks, I was able to reproduce the problem. This situations is interesting, in that I'm not entirely sure why CFI and TLI are behaving this way. When inspecting the lower-level components the residual differences are quite large (difference between the observed and expected moments are quite different, particularly the second-order moments), but when formed into the C2 statistic via the quadratic form these differences are somehow "washed out". So, the null model looks to fit noticeably better than I would have expected. E.g.,

sv <- mirt(dep.evaluation, model=1, pars='values')
sv$value[sv$name == 'a1'] <- 0
sv$est[sv$name == 'a1'] <- FALSE
dep.pcm.null <- mirt(dep.evaluation, model=1, pars=sv)
M2(dep.pcm.null, calcNull = FALSE)
M2(dep.pcm.null, calcNull = FALSE, type = 'C2')

It's possible this is somehow a bug with C2, so I'll keep looking into the issue. For now, I would probably ignore these two measures for your data as they don't look reliable.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Sum score reliability
messages.body_plain:
"Exactly the same as sum score" no, not at all. If you must use sum-scores then you should keep with the CTT methodology because these explicitly use the implied weights of 1 in their reliability computations. The fscores() method you demonstrate is the reliability assuming that you are going to use these factor-score values as the total scores instead, along with their associated SEs. HTH.

Phil

>
> 1.) In your examples, you've set constraints on item parameters. Does this allow us to make inferences on the trajectory of the latent construct over time (i.e., is this equivalent to equating)?

Yes. In these type of situations you typically have to make the assumption that either a) the individuals are changing and it the items that remain fixed, or b) it's the items that are changing, and the individuals are fixed. If they both change then there's a type of indeterminacy which occurs, making it impossible to chase down the exact behaviour without some extra work/information.

> 2.) Is it justifiable to set the constraints on parameters? I imagine that you would have to compute a constrained model and a non-constrained model and compare them. In that case, how would we proceed if the models differ significantly?

Through a lot of work. It's a push-and-pull system with longitudinal data, so it's hard for me to answer this question solidly without being an expert in the empirical domain. Sorry.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
messages.subject_clean: Scaling a questionnaire over the years
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

Thank you for your answers.

On Thursday, August 30, 2018 at 3:47:14 AM UTC+1, Phil Chalmers wrote:
>
> On Tue, Aug 28, 2018 at 10:48 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear Phil,
> >
> > I think I understood why the change in the parameters doesn't necessarily tell us that there is measurement invariance. However, I am still a bit confused about the longitudinal models in your example and I would like to ask for your help again. Specifically, I have these questions:
> >
> > 1.) In your examples, you've set constraints on item parameters. Does this allow us to make inferences on the trajectory of the latent construct over time (i.e., is this equivalent to equating)?
>
> Yes. In these type of situations you typically have to make the assumption that either a) the individuals are changing and it the items that remain fixed, or b) it's the items that are changing, and the individuals are fixed. If they both change then there's a type of indeterminacy which occurs, making it impossible to chase down the exact behaviour without some extra work/information.
>
> > 2.) Is it justifiable to set the constraints on parameters? I imagine that you would have to compute a constrained model and a non-constrained model and compare them. In that case, how would we proceed if the models differ significantly?
>
> Through a lot of work. It's a push-and-pull system with longitudinal data, so it's hard for me to answer this question solidly without being an expert in the empirical domain. Sorry.
>
> Phil
>
>
> >
> > On Saturday, August 25, 2018 at 10:40:44 PM UTC+1, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> > > Just because the item parameters and latent trait values are independent does not mean that their scale is constant. This is why IRT models often set the latent trait identification to have a mean of 0, variance of 1 (same problem occurs in SEM). If some other values were chosen then these would in fact affect the item parameters. This is actually the reason why *linking* parameter sets across multiple groups is required, because any mean/variance differences will make the parameters non-equivalent.
> > >
> > > If you are still having trouble with this idea, consider playing around with the example code in the multipleGroup() function, generating data with different latent trait distributions, and see how the single group item parameters can change. Also, topics on DIF will illuminating as well. HTH.
> > >
> > > Phil
> > >
> > >
> > > On Sat, Aug 25, 2018 at 4:22 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Dear Phil,
> > > >
> > > > Thank you for the examples. I will do my best to produce such models and apply them to my data. However, I am a bit confused about the answer and I was trying to wrap my head around it. If the population-mean score of the latent trait is increasing, shouldn't that only impact the person parameter (Theta) and not the item parameters? Isn't one of the advantages of IRT over CTT that the person parameters and item parameters are independent? In other words, if the item parameters change over the years, doesn't that tell us that the very way in which people respond to items has changed (and not necessarily the person parameters/population means)?
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, August 21, 2018 at 4:15:53 AM UTC+1, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > On Sat, Aug 18, 2018 at 11:02 AM AM <mut...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > Dear Phil,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I am working with some questionnaires from several datasets that contain data collected for a long timespan (10 to 40 years). In some datasets, the responses were collected in a longitudinal manner and in some in a cross-sectional manner.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I have analyzed the data using both confirmatory factor analysis and item response theory. These analyses tell me that there is no measurement invariance. In other words, CFA tells me that the factor loadings change over the years of questionnaire administartion (they tend to increase), while IRT tells me that the item parameters also change over the years.
> > > > >
> > > > > How does this tell you there is no measurement invariance? If the properties of the population change, such as there is more variability in the latent trait distribution/mean-score increases, then changes in the observed item parameters would be expected. It's only possible to make this type of conclusion if you are certain the population latent trait values themselves should theoretically remain constant over time; otherwise, you'd have to do some item parameter equating.
> > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The papers that I have read tell me that it's not really justifiable to look at how the scores change over the years if there is no measurement invariance over time. However, I was wondering if it may somehow still be possible to do this. One thing that comes to my mind is scaling using IRT, which I know that I can do using your mirt package using the multipleGroup function in which I would specify the names of anchor items. However, the issue that I have is that there are no anchor items, or to put it more straightforward, all items are anchor items - the questionnaire did not change over the years. Therefore I was wondering if it would make sense to use the multipleGroup function (with the year as a group) and to specify all items as anchor items in order to see how the measured construct changes over the years. I would also free the latent means using mirt.model and then plot the latent means over years.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If this is not the right approach, is there anything you would recommend?
> > > > >
> > > > > Unfortunately, I don't think I'd recommend this 100%, unless under special conditions. The longitudinal aspect of the model suggests that individuals appeared in more than one time point, while in multipleGroup() the individuals are assumed to be independent. More than likely you'd have to setup some type of longitudinal model, like so: https://philchalmers.github.io/mirt/html/Longitudinal-IRT.html. This example isn't the best in that the constraints use an older format (I should replace it with the current syntax mode....but haven't found the time yet), so you'll have to try to determine what's going on from the output coefficients. Similar analyses are also possible with SEM, and if you can make the assumption that the items types are strictly ordinal (so that the graded response model is reasonable) then it may be best to start with that method before moving to IRT, primarily for estimation-based reasons. HTH.
> > > > >
> > > > > Phil

messages.body_plain:
I located the issue with the C2 values here, and it looks like there were a few missing off-diagonal components in the collapsed moments of the data matrix prior to computing the quadratic form fit statistic. The fix is on the dev version on Github. I now get the following with your code, which appears more reasonable (it looks like the IRT model fits worse in comparison to your SEM version):

           M2 df           p                    RMSEA    RMSEA_5   RMSEA_95     SRMSR       TLI       CFI

stats 34.0284 14 0.002042812 0.0588551 0.03382035 0.08421807 0.0391606 0.6856893 0.7904596

So the comparison to the null model is a little more pessimistic than the SEM approximation (this is a trend I've seen with M2* as well). Thanks again for the report.

Phil
